Unshipped work only. [Owner requirement](../specs/REQ-DX-V1.md), [scoped model and prior art](../architecture/polyglot-v1.md).

Canonical `ecosystem/name` references, historical tag ownership, one tag and release per package, per-distribution publish ordering and the redacted failure tail have shipped. [ADR 12](../adr/0012-canonical-distribution-release-ownership.md) records them.

## Scope and guardrails

- Rust/Cargo, npm/pnpm and Python/PyPI, including napi-rs layouts. Co-located Cargo/Maturin is after v1; separate-directory Cargo and Python packages are supported. Go and NuGet are architecture examples only.
- Native tools and CI own building, packing and authentication. No universal package manager, build scheduler, public plugin platform or cross-registry transaction.
- Committed release authority and provider-observed recovery with no execution journal. Only `execute` receives registry secrets; the repo has no GitHub Environment or reviewer gate.

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

When to use this:
Reading a checkpoint is free: with no flags, or with --json, --full,
--transcript or --raw-transcript, this only reads and is safe to run
whenever you need the context. --generate is the exception — it writes a
summary onto the checkpoint and spends tokens with the summary provider,
so pass it only when the user asked for a summary. To see what subagents
did, read "tasks" in --json, then stream one subagent's transcript with
--transcript --task <tool_use_id>.

Current repo: gh/orin-dx/wisp-plugins  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

Flags:
  -c, --checkpoint string             Explain a specific checkpoint (ID or prefix)
      --commit string                 Explain a specific commit (SHA or ref, "commit-ish")
      --force                         Regenerate summary even if one already exists (requires --generate)
      --full                          Show full parsed transcript (all prompts/responses)
      --generate                      Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
      --insecure-http-auth            Allow plain-HTTP auth for --repo (local dev only)
      --json                          Output metadata as JSON (no transcript bytes)
      --limit int                     Cap the list view at N checkpoints (default: 100). Only meaningful with --json.
      --no-pager                      Disable pager output
      --raw-transcript                Show raw transcript file (JSONL format)
      --repo string                   Explain a checkpoint owned by another repo (gh/owner/name, et/project/repo, entire://<host>/gh/<owner>/<repo>, or entire://<host>/et/<project>/<repo>), read from that repo's Entire API
      --search-all                    Search all commits (no branch/depth limit, may be slow)
      --session string                Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)
      --session-index int             Session index within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based, defaults to latest) (default -1)
  -s, --short                         Show summary only (omit prompts and files)
      --summary-timeout-seconds int   Hard deadline in seconds for --generate summary generation; overrides summary_timeout_seconds setting. 0 = use setting; if setting is also unset or 0, no automatic deadline applies.
      --task string                   Subagent task (tool_use_id or agent_id) whose stored transcript --transcript streams
      --transcript                    Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes to stdout (a session's, or a subagent's with --task)

Inherited flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)
entire search — Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using hybrid search (semantic + keyword),
powered by the Entire search service.

Requires authentication via 'entire login' (GitHub device flow).

By default, results are scoped to the current repository. Use --all-repos to
search across all accessible repos.

Run without arguments to open an interactive search. Results are
displayed in an interactive table. Use --json for machine-readable output,
and add --compact for a trimmed per-result shape suited to agents (implies
--json): id, type, repo, branch, author, date, files touched, score, match
snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (repo hits add
description and checkpoint count). Fetch full detail
for a single result with 'entire checkpoint explain <id>', or add --full to
that command to pull the checkpoint's entire session transcript. For a
checkpoint or commit hit from another repo, add --repo gh/<owner>/<repo> for
a GitHub mirror or --repo et/<project>/<repo> for an Entire-native repo. The
forge prefix is required, and the hit's id must be a full checkpoint ID (12-char hex or 26-char ULID) or a full commit SHA
(a SHA is resolved to its checkpoint by that repo's Entire API). Prefixes
cannot be resolved in another repo. This is unrelated to this command's
--repo filter below.

CLI queries also support inline filters like author:<name>, date:<week|month>,
branch:<name>, repo:<owner/name>, and repo:* to search all accessible repos.

Examples:
entire search "retry backoff" --json
  entire search "retry backoff" --json --compact
  entire search "auth timeout author:alice date:week"
  entire search --code "parseToken"

Current repo: gh/orin-dx/wisp-plugins  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

Flags:
      --all-repos        Search all accessible repos instead of just the current one
      --author string    Filter by author name
      --branch string    Filter by branch name
      --case-sensitive   Case-sensitive code search (only with --code)
      --code             Search code content across repositories
      --compact          Trimmed JSON output for agents: id, repo, files touched, score, match snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (implies --json)
      --date string      Filter by time period (week or month)
      --json             Output as JSON
      --limit int        Maximum number of results (per page for checkpoint search, total for --code) (default 10)
      --page int         Page number (1-based) (default 1)
      --repo strings     Filter by repository (gh/owner/repo, et/proj/repo, owner/repo, ULID, or *); repeatable and comma-separated for multiple repos

Inherited flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

2	
3	PLease evaluate the work we've done. The current state of our codebase, architecture and semantic model against the overall goals of callisto and how it compares to our competition (changesets, knope, nx release and release please).

7	We're working on callisto's road to v1. There is a doc file with that. I also want you to understand the last week's worth of PRs and what we've been tackling.
8	
9	PLease evaluate the work we've done. The current state of our codebase, architecture and semantic model against the overall goals of callisto and how it compares to our competition (changesets, knope, nx release and release please).
10	
11	---
12	
13	Claude found this that you seem to have missed:
14	
15	No, don't merge #113. It won't release anything, because the Release workflow on main is broken and #113 is stale.
16	
17	- The failure: the Release workflow has failed on every merge since #166 (the runs for #166, #167 and #168). It dies in the "Create or update the Callisto release PR" step with E281 --decision is not valid JSON: unknown field command.
18	- The cause: #166 put release-pr decide --format json output inside the shared JSON wrapper, which adds command and dryRun fields. create-or-update-release-pr.sh passes that output straight to release-pr verify --decision, which rejects fields it doesn't know. No test runs that pair: the binary contract test calls decide but never passes the result to verify.
19	- #113 is out of date: it was generated from #163, so it lacks #166, #167 and #168 and its release-decision.json is from before them. The bot can't refresh it until the workflow is fixed. Merging it now would publish 0.9.0 without the identity and v1 fixes.
20	- The publish path looks safe from the same bug: release plan, artifact-manifest and release write their intent, manifest and receipt files without the wrapper, so it shouldn't recur there. I've only read the code, though; the publish jobs haven't run since #166.

Claude found this that you seem to have missed:

No, don't merge #113. It won't release anything, because the Release workflow on main is broken and #113 is stale.

- The failure: the Release workflow has failed on every merge since #166 (the runs for #166, #167 and #168). It dies in the "Create or update the Callisto release PR" step with E281 --decision is not valid JSON: unknown field command.
- The cause: #166 put release-pr decide --format json output inside the shared JSON wrapper, which adds command and dryRun fields. create-or-update-release-pr.sh passes that output straight to release-pr verify --decision, which rejects fields it doesn't know. No test runs that pair: the binary contract test calls decide but never passes the result to verify.
- #113 is out of date: it was generated from #163, so it lacks #166, #167 and #168 and its release-decision.json is from before them. The bot can't refresh it until the workflow is fixed. Merging it now would publish 0.9.0 without the identity and v1 fixes.
- The publish path looks safe from the same bug: release plan, artifact-manifest and release write their intent, manifest and receipt files without the wrapper, so it shouldn't recur there. I've only read the code, though; the publish jobs haven't run since #166.

Proposed fix, as one small PR done directly:
1. Make release-pr verify --decision accept decide's output as-is, ignoring the wrapper fields. That's more robust than having the script strip them.
2. Extend test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh so it pipes decide into verify.
3. Add a patch changeset.

Once that merges, the bot regenerates #113 from current main. You approve its CI and merge, and 0.9.0 goes out. Go?

On the Codex text you pasted: it's about the plugins repo (voice.md, dist/codex, versions for ranger, scribe and muse), not Callisto. I haven't acted on it. If it was meant for this session, say what you want; otherwise it probably belongs in the session working on the plugins repo.

And it also said of your input:

For v0.9, Codex's review changes nothing: E281 is the only blocker. It found the same bug independently. Its second finding is real, but it's a v1 item, not a v0.9 one.

1. Release PR workflow broken (E281): this blocks v0.9. The fix is what I proposed: verify accepts decide's output as-is, plus a test that pipes decide into verify.

2. A retried local release can skip unfinished work: real (I checked the code), but it doesn't affect v0.9.
- derive_unreleased_decision (release_decision.rs:195) skips every package whose current version already has a tag, and it counts local tags.
- If a local callisto release creates the tag and then the push or the GitHub Release fails, a retry skips that package and reports nothing left to release.
- v0.9 goes through CI, which releases exactly the packages in the committed release-decision.json, so this path isn't used.
- It is a real v1 gap. One fix: when a package's tag exists, still check its remaining steps (push, GitHub Release, assets) instead of skipping it. I haven't designed this in detail yet.

3. Its other points are v1 work, not v0.9 blockers. I haven't verified each one yet:

# Agent guide

Rules for AI agents working in this repo.

## Crates

| Crate | License | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| callisto-model | MIT | none |
| callisto-manifests | FSL-1.1-MIT | model |
| callisto-graph | FSL-1.1-MIT | model, manifests |
| callisto-cli | FSL-1.1-MIT | model, manifests, graph |
| callisto-fixtures | FSL-1.1-MIT | model (dev-only) |

- `callisto-model` (MIT) must never depend on an FSL crate.
- Check with `grep -H "^license" crates/*/Cargo.toml` after adding or moving a crate.

## Commands

- Full pipeline: `just ci` (includes the 90% coverage gate). `just test`, `just lint`, `just fmt`.
- Scoped iteration: one `cargo test -p <crate>` or `cargo clippy -p <crate> --all-targets -- -D warnings` at a time.
  - Not `moon run <project>:test`: its per-project fan-out serializes on `target/`'s build lock.
  - Never run cargo builds in parallel.
- Changesets: `callisto add --package callisto-cli:<bump> --summary "..."` (non-interactive). Target `callisto-cli`: its changelog is the one users read. One changeset per user-visible topic, written as the changelog entry: what the user sees now, no internal names or mechanism.
- Never `git checkout -- Cargo.lock` as cleanup. A lockfile diff means investigate, not discard.

## Invariants

1. Safe Rust only: `unsafe_code = "forbid"`.
2. Manifest edits preserve format: `toml_edit` for TOML; JSON keeps key order and fingerprinted indentation. No regex or line edits.
3. File writes go through `callisto_model::atomic::atomic_write`.
4. User-facing errors derive `miette::Diagnostic` with a code and a fix.
5. No emojis in docs or code.
6. No cargo features in shipped crates; behaviour is chosen at runtime (#143). The dev-only `callisto-model/test-util` feature is the exception.

## Fixing bugs

- Grep for structurally identical code (same algorithm, other file, ecosystem or mode). A sibling with the same defect is in scope now.
- N copies of one logic: unify to one implementation rather than patching each.
- A deliberately deferred sibling gets an explicit record: changeset note, tracked follow-up or code comment.
- A new shared helper migrates every call site in the same change, or the rest are tracked.

## Specs and plans

- Specs (`spec@1`) live in `docs/specs/`, one per area, current behavior only. Change the spec in the same PR as the behavior. No history, rationale or revision notes.
- This repo's release workflow has no GitHub Environment or reviewer gate and only `execute` gets registry secrets (owner policy, enforced by `.github/tests/verify-release-workflow-policy.sh`). Never add one.
- Read `ARCHITECTURE.md` and the matching `docs/architecture/` topic before changing behavior in an area.
- Read `docs/adr/README.md` before changing release flow, Git access, publishing, distribution, platform packages or manifest writes. Reversing an ADR needs a new ADR the owner accepts.
- Plans (`plan@1`) live in `docs/projects/`. Delete a plan once its work ships.
- Code never cites specs: no spec IDs, criterion IDs, section numbers or track names in comments, test names or messages. Describe the behavior instead.
- A requirement the owner didn't state is a judgment call. Get owner confirmation before it gates anything.

## Writing

- Succinct: short sentences, bullets, tables. No backstory, hedging or filler.
- Never hard-wrap Markdown or PR bodies: one line per paragraph.
- Code comments: one short line, only for a non-obvious why. Wrap at 120 columns (`rustfmt.toml`). No history ("used to", "previously"): git records it.
- No claude.ai session links in commits, PRs or files.

# Adversarial review: October 14–21

**Recommendation:** merge [#293](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/293) to restore release verification, then regenerate [#248](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/248) before merging it. Hold [#290](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/290) and its dependent PRs until the release-source guard covers the cases below.

I reviewed all six open PRs, the current `origin/main` release and identity paths, uncommitted files across the worktrees, the architecture and ADRs, and the latest release workflow failure. I reproduced two Git-history edge cases in isolated repositories. This is a prioritized review of reachable risks; I did not execute a live registry publication or inspect every line of the week’s merged commits.

## Findings

| Priority | Finding | Evidence and consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Release blocker** | **The green version PR is stale.** | [#248](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/248) consumes 15 changesets and its 0.12.0 changelog describes those changes. Current `main` has **32** changesets, including report and CLI breaking changes absent from that changelog. Merging the PR as it stands would ship the newer code without describing it in 0.12.0 and leave 17 changesets to trigger a later release for code already shipped. Its 12 checks pass, but the [latest release workflow](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/39696020661) failed in tests because `cargo-http-registry` was missing; the PR refresh job was skipped. #293 supplies that tool and currently has passing checks. |
| **High** | **#290 does not reliably bind a published version to its source commit.** | Its [version lookup](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/d08baad248b7dd714cc01aa2b5687e808bdb6a73/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/version_commit.rs#L23) reads only the first canonical manifest’s **literal** version. A Cargo member using `version.workspace = true` yields no version commit, so a later source edit can still be tagged after the registry version is adopted. A manifest move makes the move commit appear to have set the version; my Git reproduction found zero “newer” commits even when the move changed source bytes. A change made only in a merge resolution is also missed because the shared Git history query excludes merge commits; my reproduction showed a changed package tree and zero counted commits. These are reachable forms of the mismatch #290 intends to stop. |
| **High** | **#290 turns an uncertain precheck into permission to continue.** | [ `published_packages`](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/d08baad248b7dd714cc01aa2b5687e808bdb6a73/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/capability.rs#L345) returns only a set and drops provider errors and indeterminate observations. If that call fails transiently, the guard proceeds. The [executor’s later preflight](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/d08baad248b7dd714cc01aa2b5687e808bdb6a73/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs#L38) can then observe the version as exact, adopt it, and continue to tag the later commit. Propagating the error helps, but the source check must also be tied to the executor’s authoritative observation so two reads cannot disagree safely. |
| **Medium** | **The new E176 message still loses operation identity.** | [#291’s `Display` implementation](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/7d215456d28ce7063335e9e484e5fc632482da35/crates/callisto-model/src/release/operation.rs#L316) omits the registry key, artifact slot, and platform name. Two uploads for the same package and version therefore print the same operation in an indeterminate-observation error, although the durable operation IDs differ. Include the safe identifying field for each role and test two otherwise identical operations. |
| **Local work, high if unintended** | **Entire is now configured to sync session records to a public remote.** | The uncommitted [`.entire/settings.json`](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.entire/settings.json:9) changes `push_sessions` from false to true and enables checkpoint pushes. `entire status` identifies `origin` as the sync destination, and the GitHub repository is public. Entire’s [storage documentation](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/sessions-and-checkpoints.md) says pushed checkpoints contain metadata, prompts, and redacted transcripts. I found no evidence that this change has already uploaded this session. Decide explicitly whether public session provenance is intended before the next push; otherwise keep syncing off or use an approved private destination. |
| **Local test debt** | **The untracked selector test cannot serve as a current regression gate.** | The [test file](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/wf_cd627354-1a0-2/crates/callisto-cli/tests/status_version_selector_tests.rs:180) sits on a branch older than current `main`. It expects colon selectors and bare report IDs, which current `main` rejects or emits differently, and six discrepancy tests are ignored. Rebase it, update the current contract, and turn remaining real discrepancies into active tests or explicitly tracked gaps before adding it to CI. |

## The recurring issue

Several fixes this week correctly stopped treating **failure as absence**. #290 reintroduces that pattern in its ignored provider result, ignored historical parse result, and `unwrap_or(None)` on a parent-version read. Search sibling release and history paths for the same conversion and require each to distinguish *absent*, *known exact*, and *unknown*.

A second pattern is using a **projection of authority** as authority itself. A manifest path and version string stand in for the release source; a shortened display string stands in for an operation ID; green checks on an old PR stand in for a current release decision. The release model already has exact source and operation identities. The local route needs a check that preserves those identities through observation and execution, with a defined outcome when source provenance cannot be established.

The history guard also has a performance trap: it obtains the entire manifest commit list and only then takes 100 entries. That limit neither bounds the Git walk nor makes an older version commit safe to ignore. Resolve provenance with a bounded, explicit **unknown** outcome, or remove the silent limit; measure the Git calls on a large workspace.

## Recommended order

1. Merge #293, confirm the release workflow passes on `main`, and regenerate #248. Check that its decision, changelog, consumed changesets, and checks reflect current `main` before release.
2. Rework #290’s local release guard around effective historical versions and an explicit source-provenance result. Test inherited Cargo versions, a moved manifest, a merge-only package edit, an observation that fails then succeeds, and history beyond the current limit. Keep the final safety decision at the executor boundary.
3. Fix #291’s diagnostic identity. Keep #292 stacked only if #290 is corrected promptly; otherwise restack the dependency update independently. #289 duplicates #292’s dependency bump.
4. Rebase the untracked test and review the Entire sync policy. `entire status --detailed` also reports Claude Code and OpenCode hooks out of date, so adding one Claude hook has not cleared the installed CLI’s drift check.

I checked two apparent issues and **did not** count them as findings: GitHub documents `$/` as valid same-repository action syntax, and the installed Entire CLI says Gemini support was retired, so removal of the Gemini hooks is intentional. No source files or existing worktree changes were edited during this review.

Callisto has made substantial progress toward v1. The architecture is coherent, the release model has a clear purpose, and the past week’s work mostly strengthens the right guarantees. I would hold v1 today because two release paths still violate the intended behavior: the managed release PR workflow currently fails, and a bare local retry can omit unfinished work.

The strongest competitive position is **dependency-aware releases across Cargo, npm, Python, and binary artifacts, with explicit source identity and recovery semantics**. Changesets-style input alone is already available elsewhere.

I reviewed the [roadmap](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/docs/projects/ROAD-TO-V1.md), [v1 requirement](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/docs/specs/REQ-DX-V1.md), architecture, implementation, and roughly 60 merged PRs from September 19–26 Pacific. The checkout is at #167; I also inspected #168’s changes on GitHub.

The week’s work follows a coherent direction:

- **Release correctness:** immutable intent, provider observation, recovery without persisted execution state, consistent tag identity, and assets gating product publication. [#101](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/101), [#124](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/124), [#154](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/154).
- **A simpler product:** eight visible commands, one release verb, status showing actual planned bumps, and setup that detects facts and asks intent. Removing credential preflight, shipped features, and the WASM integration also reduced maintenance burden. [#134](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/134), [#136](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/136), [#143](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/143).
- **Native ecosystem correctness:** fixed groups and prereleases, dependency floors, lockfile refreshes, PEP 440 snapshots, and Changesets input compatibility. These address whether the resulting repository actually works with its native tools. [#156](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/156), [#158](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/158), [#161](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/161), [#166](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/166).
- **Identity and maintainability:** one selector resolver, directory identity, historical ownership checks, four published crates, and typed diagnostics. [#160](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/160), [#157](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/157), [#168](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/168).

My assessment is that this was valuable consolidation and correction. The recurring weakness is that individually sound changes can still break their composition.

The four-crate structure is reasonable. Manifest editing, graph policy, and CLI presentation remain separated; dependencies point downward. Consolidation reduces packaging overhead without requiring another decomposition before v1. One naming qualification matters: `callisto-model` now contains Git and file I/O as well as domain types, so it is a foundational crate rather than a purely inert model. That is manageable when documented clearly. [Architecture](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/ARCHITECTURE.md:25).

The semantic model’s best feature is its separation of responsibilities. A package owns a version and changelog; native release identities identify its registry publications; an artifact represents produced bytes; the product determines their GitHub Release destination. The decision records what will release, while intent records how those effects depend on each other. This handles a Cargo/npm package or an asset built by one package and distributed through another without inventing independent versions for every output. [Package model](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/package.rs:14), [release derivation](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/derive.rs:485).

Identity is also improving, but the wording currently overstates the implementation. `PackageKey` represents directory identity; most in-run maps still use `PackageId`, deliberately. #168 preserves earlier release history through ownership checks, while new default tags use the qualified display ID after promotion. “Promotion is display-only” therefore needs qualification: ownership remains stable, but newly generated tag names can change. [Accepted ADR](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/8ef9aa5a4fc01242221fa59dd4cbcb4893794778/docs/adr/0011-directory-keyed-package-identity.md).

The release executor is particularly strong. It distinguishes absence, matching effects, conflicts, and uncertainty; success requires observed evidence; prerequisites control ordering; receipts come from recorded execution evidence. The simulator tests recovery across faults. Those are substantive engineering advantages. The assurance still depends on what each provider proves: registry adoption currently establishes that a version exists, with no package checksum, while binary assets have stronger byte identity checks. [Observations](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/release_observation.rs:23), [executor](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs:26).

Two issues deserve immediate attention:

1. **The release PR workflow is broken on latest main.** `release-pr decide` emits `command` and `dryRun`; the action passes that output unchanged to `release-pr verify`, whose strict input type rejects those fields with E281. I reproduced this using the compiled CLI. Latest main has green CI but a [failed Release run](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/36281315129). The contract tests check jq extraction without exercising this real producer-to-consumer handoff. [Producer](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release_pr.rs:79), [consumer](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release_pr.rs:47).

2. **Bare local release recovery loses unfinished packages after tag creation.** The local route selects packages by tag absence. If tag creation succeeds and its push—or a subsequent forge operation—fails, the next bare release excludes that package. It can report “Nothing to release” despite unfinished effects. CI retains its committed roster and can recover through the executor. This is a reachable code-path finding; I verified the tag-based exclusion with the existing test, but did not dynamically inject the complete failure sequence. [Selection](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:195), [tag effect](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/tag.rs:72).

Against the competitors, the comparison is:

| Tool | Existing strength | Callisto’s opportunity and limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Changesets** | Explicit change files, dependency-aware versioning, fixed/linked groups, prereleases. Its documented non-npm approach still requires `package.json`. [Docs](https://changesets.dev/guide/beyond-npm). | Native Cargo/Python manifests and coordinated publication are meaningful advantages. Accepting change files does not establish configuration or behavioral equivalence; Callisto currently warns about discarded configuration keys. |
| **Knope** | Changesets and commit inference, multiple versioned files, automatic workspace detection, configurable workflows, and draft–upload–publish release assets. [Defaults](https://knope.tech/reference/default-config/), [releases](https://knope.tech/reference/config-file/steps/release/). | The closest conceptual competitor. Callisto offers more prescribed graph and recovery semantics; Knope offers broader workflow flexibility. Draft asset ordering is shared functionality. |
| **Nx Release** | Project graph integration, release groups, commit inference, first-class version-plan files, and a programmatic API. Rust publishing is documented through a plugin. [Version plans](https://nx.dev/docs/guides/nx-release/file-based-versioning-version-plans), [Rust](https://nx.dev/docs/kb/publish-rust-crates). | Callisto can appeal to repositories that want release management without adopting Nx’s workspace tooling. File-based versioning and graph awareness are already competitive requirements. |
| **Release Please** | Maintained release PRs, many language strategies, and Cargo workspace support. It explicitly leaves registry publication to other tooling. [README](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please). | Callisto’s coordinated publication and recovery cover work users otherwise assemble themselves. Release PR automation alone is shared functionality. |

That comparison supports Callisto’s design direction; it does not establish superior real-world reliability.

The remaining evidence is uneven. Native-resolution checks and real local registries are significant improvements, but Cargo/PyPI publication tests exercise less of the complete executor than npm’s test, and several checks skip when prerequisi
===== 31 assistant 15414
Yes. There are several missed system-level adjustments—not just documentation cleanup.

**E281 explains the broken release-PR refresh. Fixing it does not establish product-wide v0.9 readiness.** The broader pattern is that Callisto’s core model has advanced, but some consumers still encode older assumptions: one package has one ecosystem, a tag means release completion, and a version string carries enough semantic information.

I reviewed the week’s merged PRs and affected callers, workflows, schemas, tests, specs, and ADRs. I also built current main through #168 in an isolated snapshot and reproduced failures in temporary Git repositories. No tracked repository files changed.

## 1. The multi-manifest model is not consistently respected

This is the most important architectural finding.

Callisto correctly models one directory as one package, with several canonical manifests and native release identities. However, two execution paths still reduce that package to a single ecosystem.

**Dependency rewrites can change behavior after display-ID promotion.**

I reproduced this arrangement:

- One directory contains Cargo `app` and npm `@scope/app`.
- It depends on another dual-manifest directory containing Cargo `core` and npm `@scope/core`.
- Adding a separate npm `app` promotes the original display ID to `cargo/app`.
- Versioning then tries to rewrite the npm dependency using `core`, not `@scope/core`, and fails with E017.

The shared helper prefers the display ID’s ecosystem over the dependency edge’s actual manifest. It also serves dependency-floor and snapshot rewrites, so those siblings need the same correction. The failed version run had already written some Cargo changes; retry then encountered the partial-run guard. [Source](crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs) is [cascade.rs:160](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs:160).

**Lockfile refresh misses secondary ecosystems.**

In another dual Cargo/npm fixture, `version` successfully changed both manifests from `1.0.0` to `1.0.1`, but refreshed only Cargo’s lockfile. The npm lockfile remained at `1.0.0`.

The implementation selects one ecosystem per bump—even when that bump has several manifest writes. That undermines #158’s native-resolution guarantee. [apply.rs:368](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:368)

The structural correction is straightforward: derive ecosystem context from each actual manifest or write target. A display/selector prefix must not choose execution semantics. This does **not** require re-keying every in-memory map by `PackageKey`.

## 2. Release completion is still confused with intermediate progress

The previously identified retry bug is broader than “local releases.”

After tag creation succeeds but push or GitHub Release creation fails, bare `release` derives a new roster, sees the tag, and excludes the entire package. I reproduced:

1. First release fails during push.
2. The local annotated tag remains.
3. The identical retry exits successfully with “Nothing to release.”
4. No successful receipt exists.

The generated **simple customer workflow** uses this same bare-release path. Callisto’s own durable workflow retains the committed roster, so its selection path avoids this particular problem. [release_decision.rs:195](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:195), [init.rs:785](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/init.rs:785)

There is a related multi-manifest ordering problem.

For a package publishing to Cargo, npm, and GitHub, the actual generated operation order allowed:

`Cargo publish → shared tag → GitHub release → npm publish`

The tag prerequisites include only that registry identity’s publishes, although both identities use the same physical tag and GitHub release. An npm failure can therefore leave a publicly visible release marker for an incompletely published package. The tag-based selector then compounds the problem on retry. This was confirmed from the generated DAG and executor ordering; I did not publish to live registries. [derive.rs:380](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/derive.rs:380)

The missing distinction is between:

- The directory-level package.
- Each native registry identity.
- Shared physical tag/forge effects.
- Completion of the whole required release.

Those should be reconciled as one repair, not separate conditional patches.

## 3. Failed versioning can lose its recoverable input

This is an additional recovery defect, beyond release retries.

I ran `callisto add`, leaving its newly created changeset untracked, then injected a lockfile-refresh failure during `version --emit-decision`.

The result was:

- Manifest and changelog written.
- Changeset deleted.
- Lock refresh failed with E208.
- No release decision written.
- Changes remained unstaged.

The diagnostic recommends rerunning `version`. But:

- Bare retry exits successfully with no pending changesets.
- Retry with `--emit-decision` fails with E160 because the roster is empty.

Changeset deletion precedes the fallible refresh/staging steps. Meanwhile, partial-run detection checks changesets at HEAD or staged manifests, missing this interrupted state. [apply.rs:328](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:328), [version.rs:313](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/version.rs:313)

The agreed no-journal policy can remain. But inputs must remain recoverable, interrupted states must be detected consistently, and recovery instructions must describe an operation the CLI can actually perform.

## 4. Python version semantics do not survive storage

Two independently reproduced failures share one cause: stable strings such as `1.0.1` are valid under both SemVer and PEP 440.

**Committed release decisions fail verification.**

Python versioning successfully emitted and committed a decision for `1.0.1`. `release plan` then rejected it with E165: manifest version does not match the claimed version—even though both strings were `1.0.1`.

The decision decoder reconstructed SemVer; the historical Python manifest reader reconstructed PEP 440. Their typed versions were unequal.

**Stable Python prerelease baselines fail the next bump.**

`pre enter beta` succeeded from a stable Python version. After adding a patch changeset, `version` failed with E037 because the stored baseline had reloaded as SemVer while the bump operation required PEP 440.

[Version decoding](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/version.rs:163), [prerelease decoding](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/format/pre.rs:84)

The model already carries grammar, and release identities already carry ecosystem. The gap is context-aware decoding. Fix the decision and prerelease consumers together, then audit the other persisted version-bearing contracts. Globally changing the parser’s preference—or comparing only rendered strings—would conceal the semantic problem.

## 5. Versioning supports outputs that release verification rejects

Two further end-to-end mismatches:

**Inherited Cargo versions.** `version` correctly updated `[workspace.package].version`, emitted the member’s decision, and updated its changelog. After committing, `release plan` failed with E164 because the member manifest had no literal version.

Fixing it does not establish product-wide v0.9 readiness.** The broader pattern is that Callisto’s core model has advanced, but some consumers still encode older assumptions: one package has one ecosystem, a tag means release completion, and a version string carries enough semantic information.

I reviewed the week’s merged PRs and affected callers, workflows, schemas, tests, specs, and ADRs. I also built current main through #168 in an isolated snapshot and reproduced failures in temporary Git repositories. No tracked repository files changed.

## 1. The multi-manifest model is not consistently respected

This is the most important architectural finding.

Callisto correctly models one directory as one package, with several canonical manifests and native release identities. However, two execution paths still reduce that package to a single ecosystem.

**Dependency rewrites can change behavior after display-ID promotion.**

I reproduced this arrangement:

- One directory contains Cargo `app` and npm `@scope/app`.
- It depends on another dual-manifest directory containing Cargo `core` and npm `@scope/core`.
- Adding a separate npm `app` promotes the original display ID to `cargo/app`.
- Versioning then tries to rewrite the npm dependency using `core`, not `@scope/core`, and fails with E017.

The shared helper prefers the display ID’s ecosystem over the dependency edge’s actual manifest. It also serves dependency-floor and snapshot rewrites, so those siblings need the same correction. The failed version run had already written some Cargo changes; retry then encountered the partial-run guard. [Source](crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs) is [cascade.rs:160](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs:160).

**Lockfile refresh misses secondary ecosystems.**

In another dual Cargo/npm fixture, `version` successfully changed both manifests from `1.0.0` to `1.0.1`, but refreshed only Cargo’s lockfile. The npm lockfile remained at `1.0.0`.

The structural correction is straightforward: derive ecosystem context from each actual manifest or write target. A display/selector prefix must not choose execution semantics. This does **not** require re-keying every in-memory map by `PackageKey`.

## 2. Release completion is still confused with intermediate progress

The previously identified retry bug is broader than “local releases.”

After tag creation succeeds but push or GitHub Release creation fails, bare `release` derives a new roster, sees the tag, and excludes the entire package. I reproduced:

1. First release fails during push.
2. The local annotated tag remains.
3. The identical retry exits successfully with “Nothing to release.”
4. No successful receipt exists.

The generated **simple customer workflow** uses this same bare-release path. Callisto’s own durable workflow retains the committed roster, so its selection path avoids this particular problem. [release_decision.rs:195](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:195), [init.rs:785](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/init.rs:785)

There is a related multi-manifest ordering problem.

For a package publishing to Cargo, npm, and GitHub, the actual generated operation order allowed:

`Cargo publish → shared tag → GitHub release → npm publish`

The tag prerequisites include only that registry identity’s publishes, although both identities use the same physical tag and GitHub release. An npm failure can therefore leave a publicly visible release marker for an incompletely published package. The tag-based selector then compounds the problem on retry. [derive.rs:380](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/derive.rs:380)

- The directory-level package.
- Each native registry identity.
- Shared physical tag/forge effects.
- Completion of the whole required release.

Those should be reconciled as one repair, not separate conditional patches.

This is an additional recovery defect, beyond release retries.

- Manifest and changelog written.
- Changeset deleted.
- Lock refresh failed with E208.
- No release decision written.
- Changes remained unstaged.

- Bare retry exits successfully with no pending changesets.
- Retry with `--emit-decision` fails with E160 because the roster is empty.

Two independently reproduced failures share one cause: stable strings such as `1.0.1` are valid under both SemVer and PEP 440.

`pre enter beta` succeeded from a stable Python version. After adding a patch changeset, `version` failed with E037 because the stored baseline had reloaded as SemVer while the bump operation required PEP 440.

Fix the decision and prerelease consumers together, then audit the other persisted version-bearing contracts. Globally changing the parser’s preference—or comparing only rendered strings—would conceal the semantic problem.

Two further end-to-end mismatches:

**Inherited Cargo versions.** `version` correctly updated `[workspace.package].version`, emitted the member’s decision, and updated its changelog. After committing, `release plan` failed with E164 because the member manifest had no literal version.

- Right that the missing end-to-end rehearsal is a major systemic omission.
  - Right that it would have caught most of this incident’s GitHub Actions failures earlier.
  - Right that failure to implement an already-identified safeguard is more concerning than failure to identify it.
  - Wrong or incomplete in calling the rehearsal the whole fix.
  - Potentially wrong if “build it now” means encoding the current overcomplicated workflow—including manual approval and unreachable artifact
    machinery—before correcting the target architecture.

  The correct course is to make the rehearsal one of the first implementation deliverables, but build it against the simplified release lifecycle and
  pair it with the executor correctness work. No more production releases as tests, and no more test harness that can declare success without a
  terminal, externally verified receipt.

---

FYI, for context. Don't act on it:

  # Comprehensive remediation plan

  ## Phase 0: Stabilize the current branch and stop blind reruns

  1. Merge PR #97 (https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/97) first; it fixes the Rust security advisory and currently has green checks.
  2. Rebase or update PRs #95 and #96 after #97.
  3. Merge #95 and remove required reviewers from the actual GitHub Environment settings.
  4. Merge #96 as a short-term retention improvement, explicitly documenting that it is not a durability fix.
  5. Do not initiate another blind self-release until false-success and recovery behavior are corrected or a deliberate bootstrap procedure is
     selected.

  The next coherent release may be 0.7.3. It is acceptable for 0.7.0–0.7.2 to remain unpublished if dependency constraints, tags, and registry state
  are validated before publication.

  Exit condition:

  - Security checks are green.
  - No second environment approval remains.
  - The team understands that retention is mitigation, not recovery.

  ———

  ## Phase 1: Reset the product contract

  Produce a short, binding product/architecture decision that answers:

  - Who is the primary user?
  - Which ecosystems are supported before v1?
  - Is Changesets the primary authoring model?
  - Are conventional commits supplemental or a second primary model?
  - Does Rust own actual publication? Recommended answer: yes.
  - Does CI own only scheduling and credentials? Recommended answer: yes.
  - Are binary assets required before v1?
  - What is the product-level version and tag?
  - Which existing CLI/JSON interfaces are retained before v1?

  Recommended decisions:

  - Cargo, npm, Python, and native npm coordination remain the supported scope.
  - Changesets are primary; conventional commits can generate equivalent change intent.
  - Merge of the reviewed version PR is release approval.
  - No environment reviewer gate.
  - One canonical release plan and executor.
  - Remove legacy surfaces before v1 where compatibility has no real consumer.

  Exit condition:

  - README, design document, CLI help, and actual behavior describe the same product.

  ———

  ## Phase 2: Add failing tests for every observed incident

  Before correcting the implementation, create tests that reproduce the real failures:

  1. A failed operation left Attempting, followed by a rerun.
      - It must never return zero merely because no operation is eligible.

  2. A resume on a fresh runner with no local state.
  3. A publisher succeeds remotely but the local process receives an ambiguous failure.
  4. A workflow artifact containing a hidden directory.
  5. Artifacts downloaded outside the trusted worktree.
  6. Resume after main advances.
  7. Resume after the original workflow artifact expires.
  8. Explicit version installation when the exact asset/package does not exist.
      - It must not install main.

  9. Malformed Cargo/pnpm workspace definitions.
      - They must fail closed.

  10. A complete self-release against fake registries and a bare Git remote.
  11. The same release executed twice.

  - The second execution must perform no duplicate publication and still issue a valid receipt.

  Static workflow assertions can remain, but only as supplemental lint.

  Exit condition:

  - Each historical incident has a test that fails for the original reason, not merely for a similar helper function.

  ———

  ## Phase 3: Repair executor correctness

  1. Define a provider observation interface.
  2. Observe every operation before execution.
  3. Observe again after successful or ambiguous execution.
  4. Resolve abandoned Attempting operations through external state.
  5. Treat mismatched existing state as a conflict.
  6. Require a terminal receipt before returning exit code zero.
  7. Persist the journal after every state transition.
  8. Upload the journal with if: always() for diagnostics.
  9. Make journal loss survivable by reconstructing from the plan and providers.
  10. Add an explicit recovery command targeted by commit and plan digest.

  Exit condition:

  - Killing the executor at every transition and rerunning always converges to success or a precise conflict.
  - It cannot duplicate an already completed publication.
  - It cannot report success for a partial release.

  This is the highest-priority implementation phase.

  ———

  ## Phase 4: Simplify the GitHub workflow

  Target workflow:

  Changesets
      ↓
  Version PR with immutable release plan
      ↓ review + merge
  Release executor
      ↓
  Observe → apply missing operations → verify
      ↓
  Terminal receipt

  Specific changes:

  - Treat merge as the approval.
  - Remove the reviewer environment gate.
  - Keep environment scoping only where needed for secrets.
  - Avoid a build/artifact job boundary for source-only registry releases.
  - Run binary build jobs only when the release plan contains artifact operations.
  - Add workflow_dispatch inputs for release commit and plan digest.
  - Check out the requested commit, not implicitly current main.
  - Keep artifacts out of the trusted worktree.
  - Upload execution journals and receipts independently from build artifacts.
  - Validate every restored artifact against plan digests.

  Exit condition:

  - Happy path, delayed retry, advanced main, and partial remote publication all use the same workflow and executor.

  ———

  ## Phase 5: Unify the release API and domain model

  1. Introduce exact ReleaseUnitId and ArtifactId concepts.
  2. Resolve user selectors once at the boundary.
  3. Build one release graph used by planning, CLI display, and execution.
  4. Consolidate VersionPlan, PublishPlan, ReleaseDecision, and ReleaseIntent into a clear lifecycle.
  5. Retire, remove, or make thin aliases of:
      - plan-publish
      - preview-only publish
      - filter-plan
      - standalone tag

  6. Ensure no duplicated implementation remains behind aliases.
  7. Expose JSON Schema for every stable automation artifact.
  8. Add schema-version migration or explicit rejection behavior.

  Exit condition:

  - There is one implementation that decides version, publishability, ordering, and targets.
  - All frontends call that implementation.

  ———

  ## Phase 6: Make workspace discovery authoritative and fail-closed

  1. Parse root workspace configuration once.
  2. Distinguish absent configuration from invalid configuration.
  3. Turn invalid globs into diagnostics.
  4. Turn unreadable or invalid child manifests into aggregated diagnostics.
  5. Prevent malformed configuration from broadening package membership.
  6. Include file spans and remediation in errors.
  7. Add adversarial fixtures for path normalization, nested workspaces, excludes, symlinks, and platform packages.

  Exit condition:

  - No malformed authority file can silently add packages to a release.

  ———

  ## Phase 7: Finish or defer binary distribution deliberately

  If binaries are required before v1:

  1. Derive artifact slots from the release plan.
  2. Define deterministic target matrices and filenames.
  3. Build CLI archives and callisto-moon.wasm.
  4. Generate checksums and an artifact manifest.
  5. Attest the manifest.
  6. Pass a verified-manifest capability to upload code.
  7. Create one product GitHub Release.
  8. Upload all planned assets.
  9. Make setup actions download and verify exact versions.
  10. Test installation on clean Linux, macOS, and supported downstream environments.

  If binaries are deferred:

  - Remove or hide the unreachable upload path.
  - Make setup actions use only actually supported distribution channels.
  - Stop documenting GitHub assets that are not produced.

  Exit condition:

  - A clean downstream machine can install the requested exact version, or the product clearly states that this distribution method is unsupported.

  ———

  ## Phase 8: Establish performance engineering

  1. Add representative monorepo fixtures:
      - 10 packages.
      - 100 packages.
      - Mixed Cargo/npm/Python.
      - Native npm platform packages.
      - Deep dependency cascades.

  2. Benchmark cold and warm paths separately.
  3. Add command-level performance budgets.
  4. Resolve the base commit once.
  5. Replace per-package history scans with one traversal and path-to-package mapping.
  6. Cache parsed manifests and workspace membership within a command.
  7. Profile before introducing concurrency.
  8. Replace the undocumented <10ms claim with a reproducible p50/p95 target.

  Exit condition:

  - Performance statements can be reproduced in CI from a documented fixture.
  - Status no longer scales as packages multiplied by history queries.

  ———

  ## Phase 9: Reconcile documentation and certify self-release

  1. Rewrite the README and design sections from the canonical lifecycle.
  2. Document:
      - version PR behavior
      - approval model
      - execution
      - observation and idempotence
      - recovery
      - product versus package tags
      - binary distribution

  3. Add an operator runbook for ambiguous failures.
  4. Perform two certification releases:
      - one normal self-release
      - one deliberately interrupted and resumed release

  5. Verify:
      - every expected registry version
      - package tags
      - product GitHub Release
      - assets and checksums, if supported
      - setup action installation
      - terminal receipt

  Exit condition:

  - Callisto releases itself successfully twice, including one forced recovery, before claiming the release path is reliable.

  ———

  # Suggested implementation sequence

  This should be executed as small, independently reviewable changes, approximately:

  1. Tests for false-success and Attempting recovery.
  2. Terminal-receipt enforcement.
  3. Provider observation interface.
  4. Durable/reconstructable recovery and manual target selection.
  5. Workflow simplification and removal of duplicate approval.
  6. Fail-closed workspace discovery.
  7. Release domain-model consolidation.
  8. Removal of legacy release paths.
  9. Binary distribution decision and implementation/removal.
  10. Performance work and documented budgets.
  11. Documentation reconciliation.

**Yes — this is a systemic pattern, not a one-off.** Every "contract test" for the release action under `.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/` and `.github/actions/setup-callisto/tests/` fakes `callisto`, `gh`, and `git` as bash functions. Most of them (`test_native_artifact_placement.sh`, `test_status_check_branching.sh`, `test_tag_push_force.sh`, `test_github_release_creation.sh`, etc.) use an `extract_snippet` helper that pulls the *actual* shell body out of `action.yml`, so the control-flow logic under test is real — only the external tool calls are faked, which is a reasonable boundary for testing shell logic in isolation.

The dangerous version of this is specifically: **wherever a faked `callisto` subcommand's JSON output is hand-typed instead of generated by the real binary**, because that fixture silently encodes an assumption about serde's output shape that can drift from reality with zero warning. That's exactly what happened with `release-pr decide` → `ReleasePrActionV1`.

I checked whether this is currently drifting anywhere else:
- `test_release_pr_contract.sh` — confirmed drifting (now fixed, PR #47).
- `test_publish_partial_failure_filters_plan.sh` fakes `callisto publish`/`filter-plan`/`plan-publish` output by hand too. I checked the real struct behind it (`PublishAttemptResult` in `report.rs`) — someone already got burned by this exact class of bug there and hard-coded `#[serde(rename = "errorKind")]` on that field instead of trusting `rename_all`. So that fixture currently matches reality, but by an explicit patch, not because the test would catch drift if it happened again.
- Same story for `test_native_matrix_dedup.sh` (fakes `callisto matrix` output) and `test_github_release_creation.sh` — I didn't find live drift, but none of them would notice if one appeared.

So: no other **currently-broken** instance found, but the test suite has no structural defense against this bug class recurring — it only doesn't happen to be wrong right now, in three or four other places, by luck plus one prior manual fix. If you want, I can add real-binary contract tests (like the one I just wrote) for `matrix`, `plan-publish`/`filter-plan`, and `compose-pr-body` too, so the whole action test suite stops trusting hand-typed JSON for anything that crosses the Rust→shell boundary. So `#28`'s branch and current `main` genuinely disagree on workflow files.

**Here's the actual constraint:** GitHub's automatic `GITHUB_TOKEN` used by Actions runs is hard-blocked from pushing any commit that touches `.github/workflows/*` — this isn't something you can grant via the `permissions:` block, it's enforced by GitHub's API itself for that token type, full stop. So when Callisto detects the existing managed PR's branch has drifted from `main` specifically on workflow-file content, force-pushing an updated version bump onto that same branch would hit a 403 from GitHub mid-release. Rather than fail there, the logic in `ReleasePrDecisionV1::derive` (`release_pr.rs:220-229`) deliberately chooses a different, safe path when it sees `workflow_delta_from_base = true`:

```rust
if pr.workflow_delta_from_base {
    ReleasePrActionV1::Supersede { pull_request_number: pr.number, expected_branch: ..., replacement_branch: format!("{}--{}", ..., snapshot.base_commit) }
}
```

It builds a **fresh branch off current `main`** (so it doesn't carry any stale workflow diff at all), opens a new PR from that, and closes the old one with the exact comment you saw: *"Superseded... because GitHub requires elevated workflow authority to update this generated branch."*

So: not a bug, not something my fix changed the behavior of — it's the correct, intended outcome given #28 predates the workflow rewrite. #48 is the clean replacement. Nothing to worry about here; #28 being closed with a link to #48 is exactly what should happen.

- **What the release PR contains**: never workflow files. Confirmed above.
- **What triggered supersede**: #28's branch was cut from `main` on Aug 28. Since then, PRs #38–#46 rewrote `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml` on `main` itself (1.8K → 9K, added the durable pipeline). So *`main`'s own workflow files moved forward* while #28 sat open with the old ones.

To "update" #28 in place, the script would force-push `main` + version-bump onto that same branch name — and since `main`'s workflows have since changed, that push would necessarily overwrite the branch's stale workflow files with the current ones. That's a real change to `.github/workflows/*` content on that ref, and GitHub's `GITHUB_TOKEN` categorically cannot push that, on any branch, regardless of why. So Callisto detects the situation ahead of time and cuts a brand-new branch off current `main` instead — which starts in sync with `main`'s workflows, so it never needs to touch them either.

So: release PRs still never contain workflow changes. What changed is that *upstream `main`* did, out from under a stale open PR, and that's specifically what forced the supersede instead of a plain update.

No — a rebase wouldn't have sidestepped this, and I want to be precise about why, since it's a fair thing to push back on.

The GitHub restriction isn't about *how* the branch gets updated (merge, rebase, cherry-pick, or fresh recreation) — it's purely about *whether the final pushed tree differs from what's currently on that ref at `.github/workflows/*`*. That check is content-based, not mechanism-based.

Walk through what a rebase would actually produce here: `git rebase main` on #28's branch replays its one version-bump commit on top of current `main`. The resulting tree is: current `main`'s tree + the version-bump diff. That's *exactly* the same final tree the "recreate from scratch" approach (`git switch -C` off current `main`, then commit) produces — there's no merge conflict to resolve differently, so rebase and recreate converge on the identical result.

And that resulting tree necessarily has `main`'s *current* `.github/workflows/*` content — which differs from what's sitting on the remote `callisto/version-packages` ref right now (the old, pre-#38–46 files). So pushing the rebased branch would need to overwrite `.github/workflows/*` on that ref, same as pushing the recreated one. Same wall either way: `GITHUB_TOKEN` has no `workflows` write scope — it's not something you can even grant via the workflow's `permissions:` block, unlike `contents` or `pull-requests`. It's hard-excluded from the token's permission set entirely. A PAT or GitHub App token with actual workflow-write permission could do it; the automatic token categorically can't, regardless of git plumbing.

So the fix isn't "rebase instead of recreate" — both hit the identical push rejection. The only way to update in place would be to hand the job a more privileged token, which is exactly the kind of privilege expansion the last few PRs (#39/#43/#46, "release trust"/"durable attested release") were deliberately trying to *avoid*. Superseding is the tradeoff of keeping the token minimally privileged.

  - SKILL.md (Agent Skills spec): `name` max 64 characters, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, no leading or trailing hyphen. `description` is required, non-empty, max 1024. `compatibility` is optional, max 500.     - The CLI has `skilllint rules` (filterable by platform, category and severity) and `skilllint rule <ID>`. Rule lists vary by version.

A claimed 13.9–85% drop (arXiv 2510.05381) came from a secondary page, so treat it as unverified.

Repository overviews did not help. Files help mainly for non-standard practices, and unnecessary requirements make tasks harder. # v1 verification and adversarial review (2026-10-20)

Local only, never PR it. Baseline: main `d1f0de357` (v0.11.0). Twelve read-only research passes, each against the real binary, scratch repos and source. I re-ran these myself and they reproduce: E007 (Maturin), bare-tag adoption (S3), stale prerelease range after a pre cycle (S1), pre mode failing on the managed route (E165), the `Bearer` token leak in E163, `id-token` banned outside `build-artifact` by the policy script, and `edition = "2021"`. Everything else below is an agent finding with its evidence tag, not independently re-run. Scratch evidence is under `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-g

Correction to D01-DECISIONS.md: the E101 spec and code do not disagree. Two default templates cannot collide (E100 forbids duplicate ids), so `has_default && ids.len() > 1` is equivalent to WS-ID-08. The real gap is that two packages with the same explicit `tag-template` pass silently. The stale `default_for` doc comment (`tag.rs:71`) is confirmed.

## Can we tackle all of v1?

D01 no longer blocks T06 or T08. The plan was incomplete, though: the review found defects that no task covers, and the work is about 25 PRs, not one push. Cargo builds and `just ci` stay serial.

## A. Defects in no plan task (existing contracts, start now)

| # | Defect | Evidence | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | A package renamed or lookalike adopts another package's tag; after a rename the real Cargo `foo` is treated as already tagged and never published (S3b) | Reproduced twice | High: silent skipped publish |
| A2 | The local and generated-simple routes release HEAD, not the commit that introduced the version. A crashed run at A then `release` at B tags B with code that never shipped. Concurrent runs make a rerun fail permanently with E167 whose help is wrong. The generated simple workflow has no `concurrency:` group | Reproduced (agent) | High |
| A3 | Pre-release mode fails on the managed route (E165 no changeset consumed), and `version` keeps bumping beta.0, beta.1, beta.2 with no changeset | Reproduced (me and agent) | High: prereleases only work locally |
| A4 | After a pre cycle, a dependent keeps `^2.0.0-next.0`; a later major leaves it excluding the new dependency; `version` exits 0 with only a warning. Also: an unrepresentable peer or compound range is a warning, and a Cargo compound range half-applies the tree then fails at lockfile refresh (E208, then E121 on rerun) | Reproduced (me for npm) | High: wrong published ranges |
| A5 | A foreign or already-published untagged version is adopted and tagged ("already published; skipping", then tags HEAD). No check that the registry package belongs to this repo | Reproduced (agent, `itoa`) | Medium-High |
| A6 | Snapshot: rewrites every package with no changeset, leaves dependents on stable ranges, and `release --dry-run` after it plans a real git tag and npm publish. All prereleases and snapshots publish to dist-tag `next` | Reproduced (agent) | Medium-High, one-way door (dist-tag) |
| A7 | Secret redaction is exact env value plus URL userinfo. A token not in a known variable (`Bearer npm_...`) prints in cleartext in live stderr, E163 text and the JSON error. Indeterminate observations (E176) show no tool text at all; E157 has no cause | Reproduced (me and agent) | Medium (security hygiene) |
| A8 | Dual Cargo+npm `--package` selection plans the shared tag after one publish (E1); product announcement does not wait for a plugin's publish (E2); a dependent waits on every publish of its dependency (over-serialization) | Reproduced | Medium |
| A9 | Poetry caret or tilde on a co-released dependency is not rewritten (only `==`, `~=`, `>=`, `>=,<` are); `>=0.1.0,<0.2` is rewritten to `>=0.2.0, <1`, widening past the 0.x boundary; Python dev tables are silently skipped | Reproduced (agent) | Medium |
| A10 | Real-registry tests skip silently and report as passes; the PyPI test bypasses production binding and its index is HTML (production needs JSON); the file is Linux-only | Source and reproduced | Medium: false assurance |
| A11 | A failed release cannot be inspected read-only; a publish that landed then reports E163 "retry" | Reproduced | Medium-Low |
| A12 | `version` with an unknown changeset entry leaves the file, so its resolvable entries apply again on the next run | Reproduced (agent) | Medium-Low |
| A13 | No monotonic guard: tag `libx@1.5.0` with manifest 0.1.1 plans 0.1.2 | Reproduced | Low (guard judged unsound; ownership fix covers it) |

## B. Plan tasks, verified and re-sliced

| Task | Verified state | Slices |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T06 | `from_groups` is already guarded and deprecated; `resolve_unique`, `resolve_human`, `bare` map are dead. Missed: `GroupTable::resolve` accepts an alias twice (`x-core` and `@x/core`); `[[package]]` and `[[package-set]]` rules never match a dual-manifest owner's non-primary native name; init has its own resolver; colon is also emitted (identity.rs:486, release.rs:199) | P1 delete dead code and share `validate_membership` (S); P2 colon rejection E316, strict parse, resolver split (M); P3 canonical-required config, E317, rules via the index, dogfood `callisto.toml` and docs (M-L); P4 cano
| T06-HISTORY | SYS-OWNER and SYS-DEMOTION fixed; residue is A1 | A: name check plus G2 (S); B: gate bare and promoted adoption, `version_is_tagged` check, status diagnostic, fixture churn (M-L); C: batched reads only if q200 with tags exceeds 1 s |
| T07 | Post-v1 (#251) | none |
| T08 | A8 | E1 expansion in `expand_selection` (S); E2 edge (S-M); edge granularity (S-M, same file, stacked) |
| W4 | Receipts cannot hold an indeterminate observation; persisting is pointless without a failure record (reverses ADR 3) | PR1 redactor shapes, tail bound, one redacting `CommandError::failed` (S); PR2 carry bounded redacted tail through E176 and E157 (M) |
| W10 | `RewriteKey` shipped (#223). Remaining: dev-group tracking (decision) and the Poetry caret bug (fix) | S-M |
| T12 | Feasible without credentials: production `callisto release` runs against TLS devpi and Verdaccio (reproduced, no escape hatch; env CA trust plus a small TLS forwarder). Cargo unproven | T12a seven PRs (see below); T12b hosted rehearsal needs your credentials |
| T12-DX | Local floor measured: 1.6 s for init to dry-run (debug build); workflow 31 to 37 lines; hosted time unmeasured | Script plus an owner-run hosted mode |

T12a PRs: tests fail instead of skip under `CI` (S); shared TLS helper under `testing/` (M); PyPI production-path test on devpi with a partial-upload case (M); npm https binding variant (S-M); Cargo through `release execute` (M); `testing/measure-first-release.py` (S-M); `V1-VERIFICATION.md` matrix (M).

## C. 1.0 hygiene (Rust and publishing practice)

- Metadata: crates inherit only `edition` and `repository`; add `rust-version`, `keywords`, `categories`, `homepage`; per-crate `documentation`; `exclude` tests and `proptest-regressions`; real READMEs with absolute links. (S)
- MSRV is declared (1.96) but never tested; add a CI job. Edition 2021 -> 2024 and resolver 3; state an N-2 MSRV policy. Current stable is 1.99.1 (web). (S-M)
- Panic hygiene: `unwrap_used` and `expect_used` are explicitly `allow` (about 66 unwrap, 48 expect in non-test code, estimates). `#![allow(clippy::result_large_err)]` crate-wide. (M)
- `cargo-semver-checks` runs nowhere in CI; about 1,050 `pub` items across four library crates; `#[non_exhaustive]` uneven (manifests 0). #249 added a field to the public `RegistryConfig` without a Breaking note. (S-M)
- Supply chain: weekly `cargo deny` advisories, Cargo dependabot, remove `AGPL-3.0-only` allowance, dead deps (`path-slash`, `fs2`), consider `cargo auditable`. (S)
- Fuzz targets: 2 (`parse_changeset`, `parse_package_id`); none for the manifest editors. (M)
- Publishing practice (2026 norm): crates.io, npm and PyPI trusted publishing (OIDC) and PyPI attestations; GitHub immutable releases; checksum sidecars (cargo-dist default). Callisto still needs `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN`, `NPM_TOKEN` and `PYPI_TOKEN`; `.github/tests/verify-release-workflow-policy.sh` bans `id-token` outside `build-artifact` (my check) and its self-test requires `execute` to hold exactly the one secret. AGENTS.md does not ban OIDC in `execute`. First publish must be manual on crates.io and npm; the bootstrap is undocumented. Immutable releases make the documented `gh release dele
- Docs stale at 1.0: README and SECURITY.md say pre-v1; `how-callisto-works.md` lines 81-83 still list three limits that shipped; `releasing.md` retry limit and napi roster; ADRs 9 and 10 are still Proposed although shipped; `publishing.md` says to map `PYPI_TOKEN` to `TWINE_PASSWORD` though the action does; `init`/`--help` banner says "Rust workspaces"; E227 help still advertises `cargo:pkg`.
- Spec drift: about 13 of about 95 sampled criteria are false or partly true (14%). Examples: dirty worktree is E267 and shallow clone is E266, not E051; VER-CS-07 cites E049, which does not exist; VER-AGG-03 says `version` warns on an unknown package and it does not; MX-OUT-03 says matrix JSON has no `command` key and it does; VER-APPLY-14 says "existing lockfile" but `version` creates one; decision `edgeKind` spells `"Runtime"` vs `"peer"`. Error codes: 259 in docs and code match exactly; 154 are in no spec; 4 documented codes are never constructed (E050, E161, E248, E253); some duplicate me
- Contracts to pin before 1.0 (one-way doors): tag format (promotion flips the namespace), report key forms, config keys (`deny_unknown_fields`, no schema version), decision file path and schema, dist-tag policy, error-code stability, action inputs, which library API is public, `schemaVersion` meaning.
- Platform coverage: release binaries are aarch64-apple, x86_64-linux gnu and musl only; no Intel mac, aarch64-linux or Windows.
- Version strategy: a fixed group of all five crates means any library break forces a CLI major; `callisto-cli:major` plans all five from 0.11.0 to 1.0.0. #248 is the 0.12.0 release (8 changesets, no status checks).

## D. Decisions needed from the owner

1. OIDC: allow `id-token: write` on `execute` (secrets optional) and change the policy script, or keep long-lived tokens for 1.0 and document it.
2. Library crates at 1.0: only `callisto-cli` at 1.0 with the libraries documented unstable and split out of the fixed group (agents' lean), or all four.
3. Pre-release mode on the managed route (A3): support it (needs a verification rule that accepts retained changesets and no empty bump churn) or document it as local-only.
4. Snapshots (A6): never tag or publish a snapshot, or add a deliberate publish path with its own dist-tag.
5. Dist-tag policy: keep `next` only and document, or derive the tag from the pre tag.
6. E1 consequence: releasing one identity of a dual package becomes impossible. Confirm.
7. T06: bump the four reports to schemaVersion 2; `[[package-set]]` globs require `eco/glob`; text tables show canonical ids; `add` keeps writing native names into changesets.
8. W4: print-only redacted tail (20 lines, 2 KiB), deny-list with shape patterns, no persisted field.
9. Managed-CI inferred-only releases: document that changesets are the sole input and make `status --check` flag pending-without-changeset for `auto` packages (lean), or let inference open the PR (an ADR 2 revision).
10. Provenance: add a bot-author check to the release workflow (one jq clause), or accept the residual risk.
11. Python dev tables: document-only, or add group tracking.
12. Floating `@v1` action tag; platform scope (Intel mac, aarch64-linux, Windows); whether to keep the under-10-minute claim or measure it hosted.
13. Credentials and placement for T12b: a separate `workflow_dispatch` workflow with its own scratch secrets (policy-clean in a copy, not merged), or an owner-run local script.

## E. Order

1. Now, no decision: A1 (ownership), A7 PR1 (redactor), A8 E1, A10 (fail-not-skip), A9 Poetry caret, hygiene PRs (metadata, MSRV job, exclude, READMEs), docs refresh plus the D01 record (ADR 12, ADRs 9 and 10).
2. After decisions 3 to 5: A2, A3, A4, A5, A6 as existing-contract repairs.
3. T06 P1 to P5, E2 and edge granularity, W4 PR2.
4. T12a, then T12b and T12-DX with your credentials.
5. Stability contract and upgrade path, spec drift fixes, ADR 12 acceptance, semver gate, OIDC if decided, release 0.12.0 (#248), then 1.0.0.

## Process notes

- Two agents ran `cargo publish` against crates.io without credentials (the plan challenger, three attempts, and the spec reviewer, once through a real `callisto release` in a scratch fixture). All failed on "no token" before any upload. Nothing was published. This broke the read-only instruction I gave.
- The harness flagged the spec reviewer's report ("Create Public Surface"). It contained no instructions; treat it as ordinary data.
- All counts that come from grep are estimates. No hosted GitHub behavior, real registry, Windows or full `just ci` run was verified.

## Validation pass (2026-10-20, my own runs, no agents)

Method: fresh binary from main `d1f0de357`; scratch repos under `scratchpad/validate*`, `verify_*`; a fake `cargo` and a local bare remote for release flows (infrastructure reused from an agent, read first); source greps for static claims.
