There are a few decisions that block safe implementation, and several others that can be settled as v1 boundaries. The key distinction is that a canonical distribution ID names a publishable output; it does not, by itself, say which outputs share a version or release. For example, `cargo/foo`, `npm/@scope/foo`, and `pypi/foo` could be three outputs owned by one source package—or three independent packages. The model needs to represent both facts explicitly.

| Decision | Recommendation | Why it narrows the system |
|---|---|---|
| **What identifies a release owner?** | For v1, use the repo-relative source root plus an explicit roster of canonical distributions. Don’t add an opaque owner ID yet. | A directory is already the natural source locator; the roster says which outputs share its version authority. If the directory moves, require an explicit mapping rather than guessing from names or dependencies. |
| **How strict are IDs?** | Require canonical slash-qualified IDs for all new references and generated records. Read old bare or colon-qualified forms only through a compatibility path when ownership is unambiguous. Ambiguity should error with the canonical replacement. | This gives users one mental model without making existing history unreadable. It also avoids a broad “accept anything that looks plausible” resolver. |
| **What happens to tags as ownership changes?** | Never rename existing tags. Continue recognizing configured legacy templates and historical tags. Pick one stable default for new tags that doesn’t change when a same-name distribution is added or removed. | The current promotion-based fallback risks making tag identity depend on today’s roster. A package should not switch tag format just because a sibling appears. A source-root move should require explicit migration. |
| **How do conflicting old and new pre-state keys migrate?** | If the bare and canonical keys resolve to the same owner and have the same version, deduplicate them. If their versions differ, fail closed and ask for correction. | The current migration path uses `or_insert`, which can silently discard one baseline. Neither “canonical always wins” nor “legacy always wins” is safe when they disagree. |
| **Which Maturin layouts are supported?** | Start with Cargo-owned dynamic versions, such as `dynamic = ["version"]`, and verify the built wheel’s metadata. Treat ambiguous static/co-located version ownership as unsupported unless explicitly declared. | Equal-looking version strings do not prove shared authority. Supporting every backend and precedence convention now would turn a focused integration into a generic build-system framework. |
| **How are Python distributions represented in the release graph?** | Treat a PyPI publication as one aggregate effect with an exact declared file set, while recording and verifying each file’s name and digest. | A wheel and sdist are multiple artifacts for one publication. Per-file evidence is valuable for retries, but exposing every file as a separate package/effect may overcomplicate the graph. |
| **Which Python indexes are in v1?** | Support public PyPI and TestPyPI first; model read/index and upload routes separately. Explicitly document private or HTML-only indexes as unsupported initially. Let Twine and user configuration handle credentials. | Index lookup and upload are distinct operations and may use different URLs. This boundary supports the common case without Callisto taking over authentication or every private-index convention. |
| **How much wire compatibility?** | Version records when their meaning changes; accept older durable records only where needed to safely replay already-committed work. Reject unsupported schemas before side effects. Don’t build a general migration framework. | Release decisions and receipts are durable authority. Compatibility should protect real replay cases, not promise to translate every historical format forever. |
| **When are packages announced?** | Keep the agreed rule: required Cargo/npm/PyPI publishes complete before the shared tag and public GitHub release. Decide separately whether a draft may be created earlier. | This keeps the public announcement from cl
===== 390 assistant 3886
Exactly. “Supports Cargo, npm, and PyPI” is a scope statement, not a reason to switch. And we shouldn’t claim a polyglot advantage just because Callisto is written in Rust: Knope already describes itself as language-agnostic and supports changesets, Cargo workspaces, and Python versioned files; Release Please has Rust and Python release types; Nx Release covers npm and Rust crate publishing. [Knope](https://knope.tech/reference/concepts/changeset/), [Release Please](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please/blob/main/README.md), [Nx Release](https://nx.dev/docs/features/manage-releases)

The defensible distinction I see is **how Callisto models and coordinates a release**, not how many ecosystems it names:

- **Changesets as explicit release input**, rather than inferring all release intent from commit history. That’s a familiar workflow, but not unique: Changesets and Knope offer it too. [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets), [Knope](https://knope.tech/reference/concepts/changeset/)
- **A native dependency-aware graph across supported ecosystems**, so version propagation and manifest updates follow actual package metadata instead of relying only on manually configured project groups. That’s a stronger candidate for a differentiator—but we should prove it across real Cargo, npm/pnpm, and Python fixtures.
- **A release plan with explicit effects and evidence**, separating “version planned,” “artifact built,” “registry publish observed,” and “public release announced.” Callisto’s intent/manifest/receipt model points in this direction. If it makes retries safer and partial releases easier to reason about, that’s compelling to release engineers.
- **One deliberate release flow**—`add → version → release`—rather than a general workflow engine or a framework people must assemble themselves. But that’s only a benefit if setup is genuinely simpler and the flow remains adaptable where users need it.

Competitors already offer substantial flexibility. Nx explicitly makes its versioning, changelog, and publishing phases customizable, and Release Please’s manifest mode handles many packages while delegating actual package publication to other automation. [Nx Release](https://nx.dev/docs/features/manage-releases), [Release Please design](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please/blob/main/docs/design.md) So I would **not** position Callisto as “more configurable,” “works with more languages,” or “one workflow for everything.”

My suggested positioning direction is:

> **Dependency-aware releases for Cargo, npm, and PyPI monorepos.**

That gives a potential user a reason to investigate Callisto, while leaving the README to explain the mechanism: changesets declare intent; Callisto analyzes native package relationships, plans version changes, and coordinates release effects. I’d use “dependency-aware” only if we can show precisely which native dependency edges affect versioning in each supported ecosystem—and where they don’t.

The architecture should support that claim, but I wouldn’t change its direction. Keep source package, release owner, ecosystem distribution, native dependency, and release effect as distinct concepts. The product advantage depends on that semantic precision. Don’t collapse everything into a generic “package,” and don’t promise arbitrary cross-language dependency inference.

The concern is readiness: the repository’s own v1 plan still lists correctness and retry gaps. A sophisticated release model is not a competitive advantage until it is reliable in the failure cases users fear most: stale plans, partial publication, retries, and history changes. I’d make “correct, inspectable recovery across the supported ecosystems” the v1 proof point, then measure whether setup is simpler than stitching together existing tools. That would give the positioning substance instead of marketing gloss.
===== 36 assistant 8674
**Yes—I would remove automatic bare/qualified ID promotion. And yes, release ordering should come from a graph—but a graph with explicit kinds of relationships, not one generic “depends on” edge.**

The distinction that matters most is: **a source project, a published package, and a release are not necessarily the same thing.**

## Canonical IDs: simpler, with one important separation

I would use qualified IDs consistently:

```text
cargo/core
npm/@acme/core
pypi/acme-core
nuget/Acme.Core
```

They should not change spelling because another package was added. New configuration, generated changesets, and machine-readable output should use these exact identities.

But one directory can produce several of those packages. Its internal identity should remain separate:

| Concept | Identity |
| --- | --- |
| Source project | Workspace directory, such as `crates/core` |
| Published distribution | `cargo/core`, `npm/@acme/core`, etc. |
| Publication | Distribution + registry destination + version |
| Shared release | Explicit owner/group of the distributions and artifacts being announced |

This makes the user-facing rule straightforward: **names are always qualified; outputs that belong together are explicitly associated.**

It also prevents the bug we found: even if a project is addressed through `cargo/app`, a dependency in its `package.json` is still an npm dependency. Qualification alone does not fix that—execution must use the actual manifest context.

Callisto already has an exact `ReleasePackageId`; I would extend that discipline rather than keep flexible matching throughout the system. [Current exact identity type](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs:45)

Because Changesets compatibility is a goal, I would retain **legacy import handling**, not wildcard identities in the core. Resolve old bare references once at the boundary, reject ambiguity, and emit canonical references thereafter. Existing tags and prerelease records need an explicit migration; removing promotion does not erase their history.

## Should npm publish before the tag and GitHub release?

**For an ordinary Callisto release, yes: all required package publications should succeed and be confirmed before its shared tag and public GitHub announcement.**

For a release with Cargo, npm, and Python outputs:

```text
Verified builds
    ├── crates.io publication ──┐
    ├── npm publication ────────┤
    └── PyPI publication ───────┘
                  │
         All required publications confirmed
                  │
             Shared release tag
                  │
        GitHub draft / asset uploads
                  │
          Publish GitHub release
                  │
             Success receipt
```

Independent publications can run concurrently; real prerequisites determine ordering. This barrier belongs to **that release unit**, not necessarily the entire workspace.

### [Medium] Failed `pre.json` deletion can leave no retry guard

- **Location:** [apply.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:543) and [version.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/version.rs:336)
- **Scenario:** A pre-release cycle contains only stable package versions and no pending changesets. `pre exit` still produces `delete_pre_json`, but no manifest or changelog writes. Apply removes `pre.json` from disk, then `git rm --cached` fails. The index still contains the staged `pre.json`, but the working-tree file that marks an active pre-release cycle is gone.
- **Why this matters:** On a fresh `version` invocation, `check_partial_run` sees no on-disk `pre.json`; if there are no pending changesets and no staged canonical-manifest change, it returns successfully. The pre-release state is no longer available for retry, and `pre exit` itself will report that pre mode is not active.
- **Evidence:** Apply can enter the deletion path with only `deferred_deletions` (lines 505, 543–565). The partial-run guard uses the working-tree `pre.json` existence check and only checks pending changesets or staged canonical manifests (version.rs lines 336–342). The existing removal-failure test covers a changeset deletion alongside a manifest bump, not this pre-state-only case.
- **Suggested coverage:** Exercise a `pre exit` plan with no bumps/changelog writes and force the final `git rm` to fail. The test should verify recovery remains possible—e.g. retain `pre.json` on disk until deletion staging succeeds, or otherwise ensure the retry guard detects the interrupted pre-state consumption.

  - PR #248 was green on 12 checks but stale: it consumed 15 changesets while main had 32.
  - PR #290's "published version left behind" guard was bypassed by a moved manifest (zero newer commits found) and by merge-only edits. It also treated a failed provider lookup as permission to continue. The reviewer reproduced two of these in isolated git repos.

  - An untracked test sat on a branch older than main and could not serve as a regression gate.
- **Evaluation and research lanes (01a0e02c, 01a0e02f-4fba, 01a0e02f-4ede):**
  - E281: `release-pr decide` output fed into `release-pr verify` fails on the extra `command`/`dryRun` fields. Main CI was green and the contract test never piped one into the other.
  - A bare local `release` retry reports "Nothing to release" after a tag exists but the push failed.
  - A dual-manifest package got the wrong rewrite key after ID promotion.
  - Lockfile refresh covered only one ecosystem.
  - Committed Python decisions failed E165 because SemVer and PEP 440 versions compared unequal.
  - Generated workflows: "generator tests are chiefly string assertions". Green self-release CI says nothing about generated consumer workflows.
- **Local review passes (V1-REVIEW-2026-10-20, 01a0e5f1-0b6d):**
  - A `Bearer npm_…` token printed in cleartext. Redaction only matched known env values and URL userinfo.
  - Real-registry tests `return` silently when a tool is missing.
  - About 14% of ~95 sampled spec criteria were false.
  - A `pre.json` deletion failure left no retry guard.
- **Redaction (15c732d1):**
  - Four credential lists had drifted apart (`NPM_CONFIG_TOKEN`, `PYPI_TOKEN`, `TWINE_USERNAME` missing from the model's list).
  - The brief named a helper, `redact_native_output`, that does not exist. The implementer caught it.
  - The fix chosen was closed-enum diagnostics, since denylist redaction leaks on any miss.

**(b) Recurring slop and defects, with user pushback**
- **Tests that cannot fail** (a33915af): a "contract test" stubbed `callisto` with hand-typed JSON.
  - User: "We're not testing if we're running the test against a stub we generate then right? What's the point of that????? WTF".
  - Claude's own account: grep/sed workflow checks were "reactive" and "never tested GitHub's actual runtime behavior".
- **Confident wrongness and arguing** (a33915af): Claude insisted that a rebase or push could not work.
  - User: "you're dumb and wrong or you're purposely being lazy and lying to me".
  - User, later: "I KNEW I WAS RIGHT! You argued with me for two days".
- **Premature "done"** (a33915af): PRs merged and CI green were reported as success while nothing had published. Claude conceded "partial confirmation collapsing into full confidence" and "asserted provenance I hadn't verified".
- **Fixing the symptom, then going shallow:** a failed incident run was patched piece by piece.
  - User: "terrible and shallow job. Codex/GPT found a lot of issues". "You are trying to blame others first instead of looking at yourself."
- **Wording slop** (a33915af): the user objected to "Durable release" as a name ("Durable still feels AI slop and icky") and to wordy comments and prose ("How can I stop you from writing wordy prose every time?").
- **Docs shallow, then wordy, then too short** (01a0e02c): "Still feels shallow", "Didn't we say no wordy prose? WTF", "Why is it pointing to internals like findings???".
- **Changelog-hostile changesets** (15c732d1): "We're consistently doing a terrible job."
- **Invented requirements:** the user wrote "The user is responsible for setting any prepublish and postpublish… We are not here to second-guess their system". Also the review-gate claim in a33915af.
- **Failure treated as absence:** failed lookups and unparsed history became "no problem". This appears in 01a16130 and 01a0e02f-4ede.
- **Projection mistaken for authority:** a green check on an old PR, a manifest path, or a shortened operation ID stood in for the real thing (01a16130).
- **Per-fix tunnel vision:** the user said Claude "lost the plot… focusing on micro fixes vs the system as a whole" (01a0e02c).
- **Process breach:** two agents ran `cargo publish` during a read-only audit (V1-REVIEW).

**(c) Process changes adopted**
- Callisto `AGENTS.md` now has:
  - A "Fixing bugs" rule: grep for structurally identical siblings, unify N copies, and record any deferral.
  - "A requirement the owner didn't state is a judgment call. Get owner confirmation".
  - "Code never cites specs".
  - A succinct-writing rule.
  - Specs describe current behavior only.
- Other changes:
  - Fresh-context, audit-scoped passes instead of fix-forward sessions (a33915af).
  - Real-binary contract tests.
  - Architecture grep-tests that are proven non-vacuous.
  - Registry tests that fail instead of skip under CI.
  - "Calibrate against reality": fake-vs-real checks, and each doc claim grepped before it is written (ad4b3461).
  - A user-proposed changeset linter (15c732d1).

**(d) Plugin mapping**
- **ranger:adversary / exit-gate:** require that the check actually ran, and that an absent, unknown or failed result is not read as "no finding". Add "failure-as-absence" and "projection-as-authority" hazards to the scan pack. Add a test that crosses a producer–consumer boundary.
- **smith:mutator / reviewer:** reject stub-fed contract tests. Require the real producer output, and a test that fails on the original defect.
- **sentinel:** a done-gate that demands the externally observed outcome (published, tagged) rather than "merged and green". Flag any claim the agent could not run.
- **scribe:auditor / verifier:** doc-claim grounding. Flag specs or docs that name symbols or error codes which do not exist (the 14% drift, `redact_native_output`, `ScopedKey`).
- **navigator:challenger:** reject briefs that name unverified helpers.
- **A plugin-wide writing-style rule, or a mason check:** forbid filler, "durable"-style vague naming, and unrequested gates.
